claim: Mesolimbic dopamine activity occasionally exhibits ramping dynamics.
source: Mesolimbic dopamine activity occasionally exhibits ramping dynamics, reigniting debate on theories of dopamine signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about observed dopamine activity patterns, supported by citations to multiple studies showing ramping dynamics.

claim: During Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning in mice, mesolimbic dopamine ramps are only observed when the inter-trial interval is short relative to the trial period.
source: Here, we show that during Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning in mice, mesolimbic dopamine ramps are only observed when the inter-trial interval is short relative to the trial period.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study, supported by data from both Pavlovian conditioning and VR navigation experiments shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Mesolimbic dopamine activity was classically thought to operate in either a 'phasic' or a 'tonic' mode.
source: Mesolimbic dopamine activity was classically thought to operate in either a 'phasic' or a 'tonic' mode (Berke, 2018; Grace, 1991; Niv et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement about classical understanding is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent evidence points to a 'quasi-phasic' mode in which mesolimbic dopamine activity exhibits ramping dynamics.
source: Yet, recent evidence points to a 'quasi-phasic' mode in which mesolimbic dopamine activity exhibits ramping dynamics (Howe et al., 2013; Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019; Collins et al., 2016; Syed et al., 2016; Engelhard et al., 2019; Guru et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Hamid et al., 2021; Hamilos et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Farrell et al., 2022; Krausz et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent studies demonstrating ramping dynamics.

claim: The discovery of ramping dopamine dynamics reignited debate on theories of dopamine function because it appeared inconsistent with the dominant theory that dopamine signaling conveys temporal difference reward prediction error.
source: This discovery reignited debate on theories of dopamine function because it appeared inconsistent with the dominant theory that dopamine signaling conveys temporal difference reward prediction error (RPE) Niv, 2013, since ramping dopamine would paradoxically be a 'predictable prediction error' (Lloyd and Dayan, 2015).
evidence: This statement explains the theoretical controversy and is supported by citations to relevant theoretical work.

claim: Recent work has hypothesized that dopamine ramps reflect the value of ongoing states, serving as a motivational signal.
source: Recent work has hypothesized that dopamine ramps reflect the value of ongoing states, serving as a motivational signal (Berke, 2018; Howe et al., 2013; Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Some researchers have argued that ramping dopamine reflects RPE under assumptions of correction of uncertainty via sensory feedback.
source: Others have argued that ramping dopamine indeed reflects RPE under some assumptions, namely correction of uncertainty via sensory feedback (Kim et al., 2020; Farrell et al., 2022; Mikhael et al., 2022), representational error (Gershman, 2014), or memory lapses (Morita and Kato, 2014).
evidence: This alternative theoretical explanation is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Some researchers have proposed that dopamine ramps reflect a causal influence of actions on rewards in instrumental tasks.
source: Still others have proposed that dopamine ramps reflect a causal influence of actions on rewards in instrumental tasks (Hamid et al., 2021).
evidence: This theoretical proposal is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is no clear understanding of why dopamine ramps appear only under some experimental conditions.
source: This debate has been exacerbated in part because there is no clear understanding of why dopamine ramps appear only under some experimental conditions.
evidence: This statement characterizes the state of the field prior to the current study.

claim: ANCCR proposes that dopamine acts as a teaching signal for causal learning by representing the Adjusted Net Contingency for Causal Relations.
source: To investigate the necessary conditions for dopamine ramps, we turned to our recent work proposing that dopamine acts as a teaching signal for causal learning by representing the Adjusted Net Contingency for Causal Relations (ANCCR; Jeong et al., 2022; Garr et al., 2024; Burke et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework used in the study, supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The crux of the ANCCR model is that learning to predict a future meaningful event can occur by looking back in time for potential causes of that event.
source: The crux of the ANCCR model is that learning to predict a future meaningful event (e.g. reward) can occur by looking back in time for potential causes of that event.
evidence: This describes a key principle of the ANCCR model.

claim: The ability to learn by looking backwards depends on how long one holds on to past events in memory.
source: Critically, the ability to learn by looking backwards depends on how long one holds on to past events in memory.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the ANCCR framework.

claim: For optimal learning, the timescale for memory maintenance should flexibly depend on 'environmental timescales' set by the overall rates of events.
source: Thus, for optimal learning, the timescale for memory maintenance should flexibly depend on 'environmental timescales' set by the overall rates of events.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle derived from the ANCCR framework.

claim: In ANCCR, the duration of a memory trace of past events is controlled with the 'eligibility trace' time constant.
source: In ANCCR, this is achieved by controlling the duration of a memory trace of past events with the 'eligibility trace' time constant (illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a mechanism in the ANCCR model, with reference to a figure illustrating the concept.

claim: When there is a high average rate of events, the eligibility trace time constant is small.
source: When there is a high average rate of events, the eligibility trace time constant is small.
evidence: This is a principle of the ANCCR model relating event rates to the eligibility trace time constant.

claim: ANCCR successfully simulated dopamine ramping dynamics assuming two conditions: a dynamic progression of cues that signal temporal proximity to reward, and a small eligibility trace time constant relative to the trial period.
source: Accordingly, we successfully simulated dopamine ramping dynamics assuming two conditions: a dynamic progression of cues that signal temporal proximity to reward, and a small eligibility trace time constant relative to the trial period (Jeong et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes prior simulation results from the ANCCR model, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Head-fixed mice learned to anticipate the sucrose reward in all four experimental conditions, as reflected by anticipatory licking.
source: In all four experimental conditions, head-fixed mice learned to anticipate the sucrose reward, as reflected by anticipatory licking (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This behavioral finding is supported by data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Simulations of ANCCR exhibit a larger cue onset response when the ITI is long.
source: In line with our earlier work, we showed that simulations of ANCCR exhibit a larger cue onset response when the ITI is long and exhibit ramps only when the ITI is short (Figure 1H).
evidence: This simulation result is shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Simulations of ANCCR exhibit ramps only when the ITI is short.
source: In line with our earlier work, we showed that simulations of ANCCR exhibit a larger cue onset response when the ITI is long and exhibit ramps only when the ITI is short (Figure 1H).
evidence: This simulation result is shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Experimentally measured mesolimbic dopamine release had a much higher cue onset response for long ITI.
source: Consistent with these simulated predictions, experimentally measured mesolimbic dopamine release had a much higher cue onset response for long ITI (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This experimental finding is supported by data shown in Figure 1I-J.

claim: Dopamine ramps were observed only when the ITI was short and the tone was dynamic.
source: Furthermore, dopamine ramps were observed only when the ITI was short and the tone was dynamic (Figure 1I and K–M, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This key experimental finding is supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Dopamine ramps appeared on the first day after transition from a long ITI/dynamic tone condition to a short ITI/dynamic tone condition.
source: Indeed, dopamine ramps—quantified by a positive slope of dopamine response vs time within trial over the last five seconds of the cue—appeared on the first day after transition from a long ITI/dynamic tone condition to a short ITI/dynamic tone condition and disappeared on the first day after transition from a short ITI/dynamic tone condition to a short ITI/fixed tone condition (Figure 1L).
evidence: This finding about the rapid appearance of ramps is supported by data in Figure 1L.

claim: Dopamine ramps disappeared on the first day after transition from a short ITI/dynamic tone condition to a short ITI/fixed tone condition.
source: Indeed, dopamine ramps—quantified by a positive slope of dopamine response vs time within trial over the last five seconds of the cue—appeared on the first day after transition from a long ITI/dynamic tone condition to a short ITI/dynamic tone condition and disappeared on the first day after transition from a short ITI/dynamic tone condition to a short ITI/fixed tone condition (Figure 1L).
evidence: This finding about the rapid disappearance of ramps is supported by data in Figure 1L.

claim: In the second cohort with counterbalanced training order, dopamine ramps were only observed in the short ITI/dynamic tone condition.
source: As with the previous cohort, dopamine ramps were only observed in the short ITI/dynamic tone condition, rapidly appearing on the first day of this condition and disappearing on the first day of the subsequent long ITI/dynamic tone condition (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This replication finding is supported by data shown in multiple figures for the second cohort.

claim: The presence of dopamine ramps during the last five seconds of the cue could not be explained by variations in behavior.
source: Critically, the presence of dopamine ramps during the last five seconds of the cue could not be explained by variations in behavior; during this period, anticipatory licking was similar across all conditions, and there was no difference in the slope of the lick rate between the dynamic tone conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This control analysis is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: There was a statistically significant trial-by-trial correlation between the previous ITI duration and the current trial's dopamine response slope in the short ITI/dynamic condition with ramps.
source: We found that there was indeed a statistically significant trial-by-trial correlation between the previous ITI duration and the current trial's dopamine response slope in the short ITI/dynamic condition with ramps, but not in the long ITI/dynamic condition without ramps (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This trial-by-trial analysis is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: A longer ITI correlates with a weaker ramp on the next trial.
source: The dependence of a trial's dopamine response slope with previous ITI was significantly negative, meaning that a longer ITI correlates with a weaker ramp on the next trial.
evidence: This interpretation of the negative correlation is based on the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The relationship between dopamine ramp slope and previous ITI was only significant for a single previous trial, and did not hold for a broader estimate of average previous ITIs.
source: This relationship was only significant for a single previous trial, however, and did not hold for a broader estimate of average previous ITIs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding about the temporal specificity of the ITI effect is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significantly negative relationship between the change in dopamine slope and change in ITI.
source: We found a significantly negative relationship between the change in dopamine slope and change in ITI (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This analysis of consecutive trial changes is supported by data in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The change in slope was significantly greater for relative decreases in ITI compared to relative increases in ITI, indicating that a relatively shorter ITI tends to have a stronger ramp.
source: Furthermore, the change in slope was significantly greater for relative decreases in ITI compared to relative increases in ITI, indicating that a relatively shorter ITI tends to have a stronger ramp (Figure 3G).
evidence: This finding about asymmetric effects of ITI changes is supported by data in Figure 3G.

claim: The eligibility trace time constant adapts rapidly to changing ITI in Pavlovian conditioning.
source: These results suggest that the eligibility trace time constant adapts rapidly to changing ITI in Pavlovian conditioning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trial-by-trial correlation results in the context of the ANCCR framework.

claim: Mice significantly increased their running speed during trial onset in the VR navigation task.
source: We found evidence that mice learned the behavioral requirement during the trial period, as they significantly increased their running speed during trial onset (Figure 4D–E) and reached a similarly high speed prior to reward in both ITI conditions (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This behavioral finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Mice reached a similarly high speed prior to reward in both ITI conditions in the VR navigation task.
source: We found evidence that mice learned the behavioral requirement during the trial period, as they significantly increased their running speed during trial onset (Figure 4D–E) and reached a similarly high speed prior to reward in both ITI conditions (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This behavioral finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: In the VR navigation task, the dopamine response to the onset of the hallway presentation was larger during the long ITI compared to the short ITI condition.
source: Consistent with the results from Pavlovian conditioning, the dopamine response to the onset of the hallway presentation was larger during the long ITI compared to the short ITI condition (Figure 4H–I), and dopamine ramps were observed only in the short ITI condition (Figure 4J–M).
evidence: This finding replicates the Pavlovian result in the VR task and is supported by data in Figure 4H-I.

claim: In the VR navigation task, dopamine ramps were observed only in the short ITI condition.
source: Consistent with the results from Pavlovian conditioning, the dopamine response to the onset of the hallway presentation was larger during the long ITI compared to the short ITI condition (Figure 4H–I), and dopamine ramps were observed only in the short ITI condition (Figure 4J–M).
evidence: This key finding replicates the Pavlovian result in the VR task and is supported by data in Figure 4J-M.

claim: In the VR navigation task, the change in the ITI resulted in a more gradual appearance or disappearance of ramps compared to Pavlovian conditioning.
source: Unlike the Pavlovian conditioning, the change in the ITI resulted in a more gradual appearance or disappearance of ramps (Figure 4L), but there was still a weak overall correlation between dopamine response slope on a trial and the previous inter-reward interval (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This comparison between tasks is supported by data shown in Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the VR navigation task, there was a weak overall correlation between dopamine response slope on a trial and the previous inter-reward interval.
source: Unlike the Pavlovian conditioning, the change in the ITI resulted in a more gradual appearance or disappearance of ramps (Figure 4L), but there was still a weak overall correlation between dopamine response slope on a trial and the previous inter-reward interval (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ITI is a simple proxy to manipulate the eligibility trace time constant, thereby modifying dopamine ramps.
source: According to ANCCR, the fundamental variable controlling the presence of ramps is the eligibility trace time constant. Based on first principles, this time constant depends on the ITI in common task designs (Appendix 1). Thus, the ITI is a simple proxy to manipulate the eligibility trace time constant, thereby modifying dopamine ramps.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results in the context of ANCCR, with reference to derivations in Appendix 1.

claim: In previous navigational tasks with dopamine ramps, there was no explicitly programmed ITI.
source: In previous navigational tasks with dopamine ramps, there was no explicitly programmed ITI (Howe et al., 2013; Guru et al., 2020; Krausz et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement about prior studies is supported by citations.

claim: The controlling of the pace of trials by highly motivated animals likely resulted in short effective ITI compared to trial duration in previous navigational tasks.
source: As such, the controlling of the pace of trials by these highly motivated animals likely resulted in short effective ITI compared to trial duration.
evidence: This is an inference about the effective ITI in prior studies based on the experimental design.

claim: An instrumental lever pressing task with dopamine ramps had no explicitly programmed ITI.
source: An instrumental lever pressing task with dopamine ramps similarly had no explicitly programmed ITI (Collins et al., 2016), and other tasks with observed ramps had short ITIs (Syed et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2020; Hamilos et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Farrell et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement about prior studies is supported by citations.

claim: Other tasks with observed ramps had short ITIs.
source: An instrumental lever pressing task with dopamine ramps similarly had no explicitly programmed ITI (Collins et al., 2016), and other tasks with observed ramps had short ITIs (Syed et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2020; Hamilos et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Farrell et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement about prior studies is supported by citations.

claim: Navigational tasks produce weaker ramps with repeated training.
source: One reported result that does not fit with a simple control of ramps by ITI is that navigational tasks produce weaker ramps with repeated training (Guru et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement about a prior finding is supported by citation.

claim: The observation that navigational tasks produce weaker ramps with repeated training is generally inconsistent with the stable ramps observed in Pavlovian conditioning across eight days.
source: These results are generally inconsistent with the stable ramps that we observed in Pavlovian conditioning across eight days (Figure 1L).
evidence: This comparison between the current results and prior findings is based on data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: When the timescales of events vary considerably, animals may use a short eligibility trace time constant to account for the potential non-stationarity of the environment.
source: A speculative explanation might be that when the timescales of events vary considerably (e.g. during early experience in instrumental tasks due to variability in action timing), animals use a short eligibility trace time constant to account for the potential non-stationarity of the environment.
evidence: This is explicitly labeled as a speculative explanation for the discrepancy with prior findings.

claim: With repeated exposure, the experienced stationarity of the environment might increase the eligibility trace time constant.
source: With repeated exposure, the experienced stationarity of the environment might increase the eligibility trace time constant, thereby complicating its relationship with the ITI.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how the eligibility trace time constant might change with experience.

claim: Repeated navigation may result in automated behavior that ignores the progress towards reward, thereby minimizing the calculation of associations of spatial locations with reward.
source: Alternatively, as suggested previously (Collins et al., 2016; Guru et al., 2020), repeated navigation may result in automated behavior that ignores the progress towards reward, thereby minimizing the calculation of associations of spatial locations with reward.
evidence: This alternative explanation is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The results that dopamine ramps occur in the short ITI/dynamic, but not fixed, tone condition corroborate the assumption that a dynamic sequence of external cues signaling temporal or spatial proximity to reward is required for dopamine ramps to occur.
source: Indeed, our results that dopamine ramps occur in the short ITI/dynamic, but not fixed, tone condition corroborate this assumption, as well as results from other Pavlovian conditioning experiments utilizing dynamic cues in a head-fixed setup (Kim et al., 2020; Mikhael et al., 2022).
evidence: This interpretation of the results is supported by the experimental data and citations to similar findings.

claim: In experiments involving freely moving animals, sensory feedback from navigating through the environment presumably functions to indicate proximity to reward.
source: In contrast, experiments involving freely moving animals do not require explicitly dynamic cues because the sensory feedback from navigating through the environment presumably functions in the same way to indicate proximity to reward.
evidence: This is an inference about how sensory feedback functions in freely moving animal experiments.

claim: Ramping dopamine dynamics can be observed even when only internal states signal reward proximity.
source: One set of observations superficially inconsistent with our assumption of the necessity of a sequence of external cues is that ramping dopamine dynamics can be observed even when only internal states signal reward proximity (e.g. timing a delayed action; Guru et al., 2020; Hamilos et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement about prior findings is supported by citations.

claim: In cases where animals are required to actively keep track of the passage of time, this strengthens an internal progression of neural states signaling temporal proximity to reward.
source: In these cases, however, animals were required to actively keep track of the passage of time, which therefore strengthens an internal progression of neural states signaling temporal proximity to reward.
evidence: This is an inference about how timing requirements affect internal state representations.

claim: Once learned, internal states could serve the role of external cues in the ANCCR framework.
source: We speculate that once learned, these internal states could serve the role of external cues in the ANCCR framework.
evidence: This is explicitly labeled as speculation about how internal states might function in ANCCR.

claim: It is possible to use the value model to explain the results if one assumes that a shorter ITI causes greater temporal discounting.
source: In the value model, dopamine is thought to represent the discounted sum of future rewards (Howe et al., 2013; Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019; Lloyd and Dayan, 2015). The shape of this value function, and thus the predicted dopamine dynamics, is determined by the discount factor, γ. If there is a low γ (i.e. greater discounting), then the corresponding value function produces a steeper ramp. Consequently, it is possible to use the value model to explain our results if one assumes that a shorter ITI causes greater temporal discounting.
evidence: This discusses how an alternative model could potentially explain the results, with citations to the value model literature.

claim: The basis for the assumption that a shorter ITI causes greater temporal discounting is unclear.
source: The basis for such an assumption is unclear, though it has been suggested that the overall temporal discounting in an environment depends on reward rates (Namboodiri et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement acknowledges uncertainty about the theoretical basis for this assumption, with citations to relevant work.

claim: There is no evidence for dopamine ramps acting as a value signal to directly increase motivation.
source: Furthermore, we do not find evidence for dopamine ramps acting as a value signal to directly increase motivation. This is because we find similar trial-related behaviors in conditions with and without dopamine ramps.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the behavioral data showing similar performance across conditions.

claim: ITI-dependent emergence of dopamine ramps for the same trial parameters provides strong constraints for the motivational role of dopamine ramps.
source: Thus, ITI-dependent emergence of dopamine ramps for the same trial parameters provides strong constraints for the motivational role of dopamine ramps.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the results for theories of dopamine function.

claim: It has been proposed that temporal discounting in the dopamine system depends on the cue-reward delay.
source: It has been proposed that temporal discounting in the dopamine system depends on the cue-reward delay (Sousa et al., 2025).
evidence: This statement about a prior proposal is supported by citation.

claim: In the current experiment, the cue-reward delay is not the key variable determining the presence of ramps; instead, it is the ITI.
source: In our experiment, however, the cue-reward delay is not the key variable determining the presence of ramps; instead, it is the ITI.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental design where cue-reward delay was held constant while ITI was varied.

claim: A spectrum of discount factors can explain diverse activity profiles of single dopamine neurons.
source: Another work has also proposed that a spectrum of discount factors can explain diverse activity profiles of single dopamine neurons (Masset et al., 2025).
evidence: This statement about a prior proposal is supported by citation.

claim: In the model by Masset et al., monotonic upward ramps were simulated using a high γ (i.e. weaker discounting).
source: Specifically, monotonic upward ramps were simulated using a high γ (i.e. weaker discounting).
evidence: This describes a specific finding from a prior model, supported by citation in the previous sentence.

claim: In the model by Masset et al., one would need to assume that shorter ITIs cause weaker temporal discounting to produce steeper ramps.
source: Therefore, in this model, one would need to assume that shorter ITIs cause weaker temporal discounting to produce steeper ramps.
evidence: This is an inference about what assumptions would be needed for this alternative model to explain the current results.

claim: The assumption needed for the Masset et al. model to explain the results is in the opposite direction as the value model.
source: Notably, this is in the opposite direction as the value model.
evidence: This is a comparison between the assumptions needed for two different alternative models.

claim: It is unclear whether any fundamental principle predicts an ITI-dependent change in temporal discounting in the dopamine system to allow RPE to explain the results.
source: Overall, it is unclear whether any fundamental principle predicts an ITI-dependent change in temporal discounting in the dopamine system to allow RPE to explain our results.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of whether alternative models have principled explanations for the results.

claim: ANCCR provides a principled and parsimonious explanation for the results.
source: While it is thus possible to rationalize our results using alternative theories of dopamine, ANCCR provides a principled and parsimonious explanation.
evidence: This is an argument for the explanatory power of ANCCR compared to alternatives.

claim: Given that the foundation of ANCCR is looking back in time for causes of rewards, differences in memory maintenance via eligibility traces will have profound implications on predicted dopamine signaling.
source: Given that the foundation of ANCCR is looking back in time for causes of rewards, it is clear that differences in memory maintenance via eligibility traces will have profound implications on predicted dopamine signaling.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the ANCCR framework.

claim: When the ITI is short and rewards are being frequently delivered, the eligibility trace time constant needs to be small.
source: For example, when the ITI is short and rewards are being frequently delivered, it intuitively makes sense that the eligibility trace time constant needs to be small; this is because the time window over which one would want to search for potentially causal cues is going to be shorter in this situation.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle of ANCCR explained through intuitive reasoning.

claim: The eligibility trace time constant adapts to the overall event rates for efficient coding.
source: We formalize this intuition by postulating that the eligibility trace time constant adapts to the overall event rates for efficient coding (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical postulate of ANCCR, with reference to formal derivations in Appendix 1.

claim: In the case of a dynamic progression of cues, the cues closer in time to the reward will have higher causal power, and thus higher ANCCR, resulting in a dopamine ramp.
source: In the case of a dynamic progression of cues, the cues closer in time to the reward will have higher causal power, and thus higher ANCCR, resulting in a dopamine ramp.
evidence: This is a prediction of the ANCCR model for the specific experimental conditions.

claim: The cue onset response in the short ITI condition is small but positive in the experiment but negative in ANCCR simulations.
source: This may explain a discrepancy between the simulations and experimental results: the cue onset response in the short ITI condition is small but positive in the experiment but negative in ANCCR.
evidence: This identifies a specific discrepancy between simulations and experimental data.

claim: The discrepancy between simulations and experimental results may be because the cue onset was already learned to be meaningful prior to the short ITI condition.
source: This discrepancy may be because the cue onset was already learned to be meaningful prior to the short ITI condition, thereby resulting in a stronger cue onset response in the experimental data.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy based on the training history.

claim: The current results provide a clear constraint for dopamine theories.
source: Regardless of such considerations, the current results provide a clear constraint for dopamine theories and demonstrate that an underappreciated experimental variable determines the emergence of mesolimbic dopamine ramps.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the theoretical implications of the findings.

claim: An underappreciated experimental variable (ITI) determines the emergence of mesolimbic dopamine ramps.
source: Regardless of such considerations, the current results provide a clear constraint for dopamine theories and demonstrate that an underappreciated experimental variable determines the emergence of mesolimbic dopamine ramps.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the main contribution of the study.

claim: A total of 27 adult wild-type C57BL/6 J mice were included in analysis across experiments.
source: Data from a total of 27 adult wild-type C57BL/6 J mice (#000664, Jackson Laboratory) were included in analysis across experiments: nine mice (four females, five males) were used for the first cohort of Pavlovian conditioning, nine mice (four females, five males) were used for the second cohort of Pavlovian conditioning, and nine mice (six females, three males) were used for the VR task.
evidence: This describes the sample size and composition for the study.

claim: Data from two additional mice were excluded from analysis.
source: Data from two additional mice were excluded from analysis: one from the Pavlovian conditioning experiment for failing to display any learning in the form of anticipatory licking and one from the VR task experiment for fiber mistargeting outside of the nucleus accumbens.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria and number of excluded subjects.

claim: Mice underwent water deprivation to increase motivation.
source: To increase motivation, mice underwent water deprivation. During deprivation, mice were weighed daily and given enough fluids to maintain ~85% of their baseline weight.
evidence: This describes a methodological procedure used in the study.

claim: A unilateral injection of 500 nL of dLight1.3b was targeted to the NAcC.
source: A unilateral injection (Nanoject III, Drummond) of 500 nL of dLight1.3b (Patriarchi et al., 2018; AAVDJ-CAG-dLight1.3b, 2.4x1013 GC/mL diluted 1:10 in sterile saline) was targeted to the NAcC using the following coordinates from bregma: AP 1.3, ML +/-1.4, DV –4.55.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for viral injection.

claim: An optic fiber was implanted 100 μm above the site of injection.
source: After viral injection, an optic fiber (NA 0.66, 400 μm, Doric Lenses) was implanted 100 μm above the site of injection.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for fiber implantation.

claim: Mice were given at least three weeks to recover before starting behavioral experiments.
source: Mice recovered and were given at least three weeks before starting behavioral experiments.
evidence: This describes the recovery period after surgery.

claim: In the long ITI conditions, the ITI was drawn from a truncated exponential distribution with a mean of 55 s, maximum of 186 s, and minimum of 6 s.
source: In the long ITI conditions, the ITI was drawn from a truncated exponential distribution with a mean of 55 s, maximum of 186 s, and minimum of 6 s.
evidence: This describes the specific parameters of the long ITI condition.

claim: The short ITIs were drawn from a truncated exponential distribution, averaging 8 s with a maximum of 12 s and minimum of 6 s.
source: The short ITIs were similarly drawn from a truncated exponential distribution, averaging 8 s with a maximum of 12 s and minimum of 6 s.
evidence: This describes the specific parameters of the short ITI condition.

claim: Mice had 100 trials per day in the short ITI conditions.
source: While mice had 100 trials per day in the short ITI conditions, long ITI sessions were capped at 40 trials due to limitations on the amount of time animals could spend in the head-fixed setup.
evidence: This describes the number of trials per session in the short ITI condition.

claim: Long ITI sessions were capped at 40 trials due to limitations on the amount of time animals could spend in the head-fixed setup.
source: While mice had 100 trials per day in the short ITI conditions, long ITI sessions were capped at 40 trials due to limitations on the amount of time animals could spend in the head-fixed setup.
evidence: This describes the number of trials per session in the long ITI condition and the rationale.

claim: For the dynamic tone conditions, the tone frequency either increased (dynamic up↑ starting at 3 kHz) or decreased (dynamic down↓ starting at 12 kHz) by 80 Hz every 200ms, for a total change of 3.2 kHz across 8 s.
source: For the dynamic tone conditions, the tone frequency either increased (dynamic up↑ starting at 3 kHz) or decreased (dynamic down↓ starting at 12 kHz) by 80 Hz every 200ms, for a total change of 3.2 kHz across 8 s.
evidence: This describes the specific parameters of the dynamic tone stimuli.

claim: The dynamic change in frequency across the 8 s was intentionally designed to indicate to the mice the temporal proximity to reward.
source: This dynamic change in frequency across the 8 s was intentionally designed to indicate to the mice the temporal proximity to reward, which is thought to be necessary for ramps to appear in a Pavlovian setting.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the dynamic tone design.

claim: Training for the VR task lasted an average of 21.4 days (range 11–38 days).
source: Training lasted an average of 21.4 days (range 11–38 days), ending once mice could consistently run down the full 67 cm virtual hallway for three consecutive days.
evidence: This describes the duration of training for the VR task.

claim: There were 50 trials per day in both the long and short ITI conditions in the VR task.
